newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Russian says NATO promises on enlargement too weak.
newsitem.headline: Russian says NATO promises on enlargement too weak.

text.p: Russia's deputy foreign minister told NATO on Friday it could not move Moscow to accept the alliance's enlargement into Eastern Europe by vowing not to put troops or nuclear weapons on new members' soil.

In a tough talk on European security at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Alexander Avdeev accused the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation of clinging to decades-old military doctrine that still saw Moscow as its most dangerous potential enemy.
He dismissed NATO's proposal to avoid deployments in any of the Eastern Europe democracies it plans to admit by 1999.

"May I stress that non-deployment of NATO structures would not suffice because circumstances may change," Avdeev told a panel discussion that included NATO Secretary General Javier Solana and British Foreign Minister Malcolm Rifkind.

"We have to envisage the possible deployment of the military system within the territory of the new members," he added, saying such a move was "almost inevitable" and would bring NATO's military might right up to Russia's borders.

"We ask how NATO is going to commit itself not to deploy forces," he added. "Is it for this year, next year, for 10 years or for eternity? And how is it going to guarantee this? With legal documents or otherwise? Declarations? Statements?"

Solana had earlier reiterated NATO's plan to embrace former Warsaw Pact satellites at its Madrid summit in July. He did not name them, but Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic lead the field of candidates with Romania and Slovenia close behind.
He stressed NATO sought to build good ties with Moscow that acknowledged Russia's importance for European security.

Avdeev said efforts to build closer ties were going well on the political and diplomatic level, but broke down when it came to military doctrine, which he alleged NATO had not changed essentially since the 1970s.
"If NATO takes on new members on the basis on military thinking from the 1970s, it gives us in Russia the impression that we are being asked to jump backward in time to 20 years ago," he said.

Rifkind said NATO was in essence an insurance policy that may not be necessary at the moment but would be hard to rebuild if now dismantled, especially if that meant loosening strong security ties between Europe and the United States.
A potential threat may come from the South rather than the East, he added, citing the possibility that Libya could threaten NATO's southern members with ballistic missiles.

And he reminded Avdeev that Europe's security situation would be very different if Russian ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky and not Boris Yeltsin had been elected president of a country that still has 10,000 nuclear warheads.
U.S. Senator John Kerry, a Democrat from Massachussetts, bluntly told Avdeev that NATO's admission of its first new members in two decades was inevitable.
"NATO is going to be enlarged. That is reality," he said, although opposition to the idea could grow in the Senate as the political and financial costs of the move become clearer.

"If we were to turn our backs on them and some time in the future things were to change in Russia, as history has proven to us they can, we would all be asking ourselves the question for years to come: Why?"
